summary: Reports on the experience of the General Area Review Team in reviewing Internet-Drafts since 2004. It covers the lessons learned over seven years, including moving from reviews before IESG telechats to reviews during IETF Last Call. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A team of volunteers reads documents and gives feedback before they are finished, like proofreaders. This reports what they learned doing that for years.

subtitle: How a volunteer review team helps ensure IETF documents are ready for publication.

tldr.problem: The IETF standards process is heavy: the General Area Director faces a large load of Internet-Drafts to review for each bi-weekly IESG telechat, sometimes over 20 documents in a single week with less than a week's notice.
tldr.mechanism: Since 2004, the General Area Review Team (Gen-ART) has assigned trusted reviewers to evaluate drafts during IETF Last Call (since 2005) and before IESG telechats. Reviewers check for clarity, architecture, security, IANA completeness, and editorial issues, giving the General AD focused feedback on problem areas.
tldr.outcome: Gen-ART reviews have improved draft quality and readiness. By having reviews done at Last Call time, 70% of reviewed drafts are ready for the telechat with no outstanding issues. The team has completed around two thousand reviews across 7+ years.

facts.label: Typical team size
facts.value: Dozen full-time, nine monthly reviewers; ideal target is 30

facts.label: Review timing
facts.value: IETF Last Call and IESG telechat

today: RFC 6385 is an Informational RFC documenting Gen-ART's experience through October 2011. The review process continues to operate and remains integral to IETF document quality assurance. Reviews are now expected during IETF Last Call, and the role has evolved to be more formal than in the original 2004 model, though it remains outside the official standards process.

sections.title: What Is Gen-ART and Why It Exists
sections.content:
The General Area Review Team (Gen-ART) was created in 2004 by the General Area Director to offload some of the IESG review burden. The review team members are trusted technical experts: many are IETF Working Group (WG) chairs, subject matter experts, and current or past Area Directors or Internet Architecture Board members.

The review team has no official role in the IETF standards process but serves at the General AD's invitation. Gen-ART is modeled on a successful review program in the Operations Directorate: quick, focused reviews close to decision time. By having a trusted group read and evaluate drafts, the General AD can concentrate on documents where reviewers raised concerns.
sections.eli5: The IETF has too many documents for one person to read thoroughly. A team of volunteers reads them instead and tells the leader which ones have problems. That way the leader can focus on the tricky ones.

sections.title: The Review Process
sections.content:
IETF Last Call reviews: Since early 2005, Gen-ART assigns reviewers during IETF Last Call (when drafts are open for public comment before IESG review). Assignments happen on Thursday evenings on a round-robin basis to ensure fair workload distribution. This gives reviewers at least one to three weeks to review a draft. The secretary makes assignments weekly, excluding reviewers who are unavailable or have conflicts.

IESG telechat reviews: When a draft appears on the IESG agenda, if it was reviewed at LC time, the original reviewer checks only that open issues were resolved (unless the draft changed). For new drafts, a reviewer is assigned using the same round-robin process.

Reviews must include a summary statement (e.g., 'ready for publication', 'has nits', 'has open issues', 'has serious issues', or 'not competent to review'). Reviewers check for architectural soundness, security, IANA considerations, clear English, correct references, and alignment with IETF architectural principles. All substantive comments are public; purely editorial comments can be sent privately if major revision is needed.
sections.eli5: Volunteers are assigned documents to read on a rotating schedule. They write comments checking for problems: Is it clear? Does it make sense? Are there security issues? Is the IANA section complete?

sections.title: Running the Review Program
sections.content:
The secretary maintains a spreadsheet tracking all reviews and assignments. Columns include the LC or telechat date, document filename (linked to the IETF tracker), assigned reviewer, review category, previous review summary, and current review summary.

For Last Call assignments, the secretary caches LC announcements and builds an assignment file using pre-prepared reviewer ordering. New I-Ds are added to the spreadsheet with links to reviews. Files are saved in HTML and sorted by date, reviewer, and document name. The process is largely manual, though a default row template minimizes data entry.

Once reviews arrive (ideally by close of business Tuesday before the telechat), the secretary uploads them, updates the spreadsheet, and sends a summary to the Gen-ART mailing list. Reviews are also sent to authors, the responsible AD, and WG chairs. The secretary occasionally creates a synopsis if the reviewer did not provide one.
sections.eli5: Someone keeps a spreadsheet of who reviewed what. Reviewers send their comments by email. The coordinator organizes everything and posts it for the Area Director to see.

sections.title: What Reviewers and Leaders Think
sections.content:
Reviewers' impressions: Team members report that they catch real problems but most drafts are solid. Comments tend to fall into three categories: editorial/grammar, editorial/clarity, and actual technical problems. The team notes fewer grammar-only comments over time, indicating improving draft quality. Reviewers appreciate the direct assignment model and find that authors are generally receptive to feedback. One reviewer noted that it is becoming rare to hear 'these folks have suffered enough' — meaning drafts are being fixed faster.

General Area Directors' impressions: ADs call Gen-ART essential. One stated: 'The reviewing load for the IESG does not scale.' With 20+ drafts on a single agenda, conscientious review by one person is impossible. The ADs see reviews as improving quality and timeliness. They note that polite, well-reasoned reviews are well-received by authors and WGs. One concern: the time crunch. Assignments go out Thursday/Friday, but the AD needs reviews by Tuesday — only three work days. Some reviewers receive 100+ page documents.

Secretaries' impressions: Serving as secretary provides insight into IETF work flow and document progression. The process is informal and somewhat fragile, depending on volunteer dedication. The secretary worries about reviewer burnout and believes adding more reviewers (to reach about 30 total) would help.
sections.eli5: Reviewers say they find real bugs and appreciate open-minded authors. The Area Directors say they could not do their job without these reviews. The person running it all worries about burning out the volunteers.

sections.title: Impact and Results
sections.content:
Gen-ART has provided reviews to 3 General Area Directors over 7+ years, completing around two thousand publicly available reviews. The team comprises roughly a dozen full-time reviewers and nine reviewers on a 'one doc per month' schedule.

Quality metrics show improvement. From 2007 data: of 250+ drafts assigned at Last Call time, 82% were reviewed. Of those completed reviews, 70% were deemed 'Ready' (no outstanding issues) at the time of the telechat. For drafts not reviewed at Last Call, only about 25% were 'Ready' at telechat time. This 45 percentage point difference demonstrates the value of early LC review.

Statistics show a trend of increased draft quality and readiness for progression by the time documents reach IESG telechat. The process has succeeded in improving document quality without becoming a roadblock.
sections.eli5: Over seven years, the team reviewed two thousand documents. Documents reviewed early (at Last Call) are much more likely to be ready for final approval than documents reviewed only at the last minute.

sections.title: Challenges and Future Improvements
sections.content:
The current review team carries a heavy workload. Full-time reviewers receive 2-3 assignments per month. Recruitment of additional reviewers would ease the load, with about 30 reviewers being an ideal team size (currently around 20 active). Adding reviewers requires minimal additional secretary workload.

The process is largely manual. Automation opportunities include: a web interface for reviewers to upload reviews (which would automatically generate emails and appear in spreadsheet links), tools to maintain reviewer availability lists, and standardized assignment logic. However, significant manual intervention will always be needed for assignment decisions to avoid conflicts of interest and ensure fairness.

The secretary's process involves many Thursday evening tasks (assignments, spreadsheet updates, file uploads) that are time-intensive. Some of this work could be delegated to volunteers.
sections.eli5: The system works but is all done by hand. Automation would help the coordinators. The workload is heavy; more volunteers would spread it out. Everything is public, so anyone can see the reviews.
